content:
Picture the corner of your notebook. It makes a right angle, a clean 90 degrees. Fold a diagonal across it, and you split that corner into two angles that still add to 90. That one move — breaking a known angle into parts — sits behind most opening geometry items on the exam. This free SAT Math Geometry practice test starts right there, with points, lines and angle pairs, then climbs toward the trickier set-ups. Scroll down for 15 Digital SAT-style MCQs, each with an instant score and a short reason.

What the SAT Math Geometry practice test covers

The Digital SAT keeps its geometry vocabulary tight, so a small list carries a lot of weight. You mostly meet these ideas, again and again:

  • Points, lines, rays and segments, and the words that name them.
  • Angle types — acute, right, obtuse and straight.
  • Complementary angles that add to 90, and supplementary angles that add to 180.
  • Vertical angles, which are always equal.
  • Linear pairs on a straight line, where the two angles add to 180.

Know these five cold and you can label any figure fast. And a labelled figure is already half the solution.

Read the figure before you read the question

Here is a habit I drill with every student. Look at the picture first. Mark the right angles, tick the equal sides, and write in any angle you already know. Then read the question. So often the answer is sitting right in the diagram, waiting for one subtraction.

Turn angle-pair words into equations

Most geometry wording is just code for a simple sum. Once you translate it, the algebra is easy. This table shows the swaps that matter most:

The question saysWhat it meansThe equation
Angles are complementaryThey add to 90°a + b = 90
Angles are supplementaryThey add to 180°a + b = 180
Angles form a linear pairOn a line, sum 180°a + b = 180
Angles are verticalThey are equala = b

Say two angles are complementary in a 3 : 7 ratio. Ten parts share 90 degrees, so one part is 9. Then the larger angle is 7 times 9, or 63 degrees. No guessing, just parts.

The mistakes that quietly cost points

Two errors show up more than any others. First, students mix up complementary and supplementary. A quick fix: C comes before S in the alphabet, and 90 comes before 180. Second, people trust a figure marked ‘not drawn to scale’. Never eyeball those. Use the given numbers and the rules, not the look of the sketch.

A quick worked example

Two angles lie on a straight line. One measures (3x + 27) degrees, the other measures 117 degrees. Because they form a linear pair, they add to 180. So (3x + 27) + 117 = 180. That gives 3x + 27 = 63, then 3x = 36, and x = 12. Notice the rhythm: name the pair, write the sum, then solve. That is the exact pattern this SAT Math Geometry practice test rewards.

quiz.title: SAT Geometry Basics Quiz
quiz.intro: Fifteen Digital SAT-style questions on points, lines and angles. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: An angle measures 143°. Which term best describes it?
questions.explanation: Angles below 90° are acute, exactly 90° right, and between 90° and 180° obtuse. 143° is obtuse.

questions.q: Two angles are supplementary and one measures 117°. What is the other angle, in degrees?
Which of these has no length, width, or thickness and shows only a location?
questions.explanation: By definition, the answer is "A point".

questions.q: The common endpoint of the two rays that form an angle is called the:
Two lines in a plane that never meet are called:
questions.explanation: By definition, the answer is "Parallel lines".

questions.q: The measures of two complementary angles are in the ratio 3 : 7. Find the larger one, in degrees.
questions.explanation: 3 + 7 = 10 parts share 90°, so one part is 9°. The larger angle: 7 × 9 = 63°.

questions.q: Angles of (3x + 27)° and 117° lie on a straight line. Solve for x.
questions.explanation: A linear pair sums to 180°: (3x + 27) + 117 = 180, so 3x + 27 = 63 and x = 12.

questions.q: Two angles are complementary and one measures 68°. What is the other angle, in degrees?
Two angles are supplementary and one measures 110°. What is the other angle, in degrees?
How many points are needed to determine exactly one straight line?
Two rays sharing a common endpoint form a:
questions.explanation: By definition, the answer is "An angle".

questions.q: A part of a line with two endpoints is called a:
questions.explanation: By definition, the answer is "Line segment".

questions.q: The measures of two supplementary angles are in the ratio 3 : 6. Find the larger one, in degrees.
questions.explanation: 3 + 6 = 9 parts share 180°, so one part is 20°. The larger angle: 6 × 20 = 120°.

questions.q: Two angles form a linear pair. One measures (4x + 20)° and the other measures 120°. What is the value of x?
questions.explanation: A linear pair sums to 180°: (4x + 20) + 120 = 180, so 4x + 20 = 60 and x = 10.

questions.q: An angle measures 136°. Which term best describes it?
questions.explanation: Angles below 90° are acute, exactly 90° right, and between 90° and 180° obtuse. 136° is obtuse.
